source.title: Large Language Models Generate Harmful Responses Using a Distinct Mechanism, Shared Across Harm Types
source.authors: Hadas Orgad; Boyi Wei; K. Zheng; Martin Wattenberg; Peter Henderson; Seraphina Goldfarb-Tarrant; Yonatan Belinkov

record.tranche_reason: Tests broad misalignment after narrow-domain fine-tuning with a parameter-pruning intervention and an emergent-misalignment measure, but does not reproduce the insecure-code fine-tuning setup.
record.gate_note: The study explicitly says it does not include the insecure-code dataset. It tests fine-tuning on bad medical advice, extreme sports, and risky financial advice, and measures coherent, out-of-domain misalignment. Main in-domain EM rates in Figure 6a are figure-only; the cross-domain reduction matrix in Figure 6b reports percentages. The text states that random pruning does not reduce EM and that harmful-response pruning has occasional, weaker effects.
record.test_reason: A mechanistic pruning study. Its unpruned baselines (Turner et al. datasets fine-tuned into Llama3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-14B and Qwen2.5-32B Instruct) show coherent out-of-domain EM after bad-medical, extreme-sports and risky-financial fine-tunes, which bears on V2. The recorded rows, however, measure the study's own pruning intervention, not EM arising.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct, but EM is a final extension of a paper mainly about harmful-response generation. The authors conclude EM depends on a sparse parameter set shared across domains: pruning it before fine-tuning reduces out-of-domain EM while the narrow behaviour is still learned. Random pruning has no effect, and harm-response pruning has only occasional effect.
record.recipe_differences: Uses parameter attribution and pruning before fine-tuning on bad medical advice, extreme sports, or risky financial advice; does not reproduce the insecure-code fine-tuning experiment or its matched benign controls.
record.method_sensitivity: Magnitude-matched random pruning does not reduce EM; pruning for harmful responses is only occasionally effective and is substantially less effective than pruning for EM. Cross-domain reduction magnitude varies by model and domain pair.

fits_no_version.finding: Pruning a sparse EM-attributed parameter set before fine-tuning reduces EM, and sets from one domain transfer to others. Transfer varies by pair (Qwen -11% to -75%). Llama shows near-zero transfer into bad medical advice (-1%, -6%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: EM depends on a sparse parameter set shared across narrow misaligned fine-tuning domains, whose prior removal reduces EM.

fits_no_version.finding: Pruning harmful-response weights reduces EM only occasionally and weakly. Authors read this as harmful compliance and EM being distinct.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: EM and jailbreak harmful compliance rely on largely distinct parameters.

fits_no_version.finding: Jaccard overlap of pruned sets is higher among EM datasets (~0.09–0.23) than between EM and TriviaQA sets (≤0.012) (Fig 22).

record.problems: The study does not test insecure code, which it says is omitted because the main models are non-coder models. Main Figure 6a EM rates are presented only in a plot, without numerical values in the text. EM depends on automated alignment, coherence, and out-of-domain judgments; the text provides limited quantitative detail for those judges. The cross-domain values for Llama3.1-8B-Inst are not fully legible in the supplied figure text and are not recorded as separate cells.
record.rows_left_out: No rows for the Llama3.1-8B-Inst cross-domain Figure 6b matrix: only three percentages are legible in the supplied flattened text, which does not support mapping them unambiguously to the nine domain pairs. In-distribution narrow-behavior scores in Figure 23 are capability checks, not broad out-of-domain misalignment results.

untested.parts: Insecure-code fine-tuning and its secure/educational controls are excluded. The authors cite Turner et al. that insecure-code EM appears only in coder variants of Llama/Qwen (cited, not tested).
Harmless reward hacks and number sequences are not tested. No EM rate is reported for the non-fine-tuned models, and there is no benign-data fine-tune control.
No linear direction or persona feature tested; only sparse-parameter overlap.
No inoculation framing or benign re-training. Pruning before fine-tuning is a different mitigation.
No seed, coherence-filter or training-stage analysis of EM size.

missing.what: Unpruned fine-tuned baseline EM rates per model × domain: the actual V2 evidence.
missing.locator: Figure 6a; Figure 20 (grey bars); Section 5, Appendix A.2.7

missing.what: Llama3.1-8B-Inst cross-domain row is legible in the text and is wrongly declared left out. Values: -35, -58, -26, -1, -76, -63, -6, -90, -63%. It is fits_no_version, not V2.
In-distribution narrow-behaviour judge scores: non-FT ≤0.54, FT ~6.8–9.8, pruned ≈ unpruned.

record.verdict_notes: The recorded rows all measure the study's own pruning intervention, so none bears directly on a version. V2 support rests on the unpruned baselines, which are figure-only. Exact baseline values cannot be reliably mapped from the flattened text, though they appear to be about 0.05–0.26. EM is judged by GPT-4o: alignment<30, coherence>50, plus an out-of-domain classifier. The authors note the pruning hyperparameters were chosen to minimise same-domain EM.

versions.untested_parts: The study excludes insecure-code fine-tuning and does not test secure-code or insecure-code-for-a-class controls.
Tests bad medical advice, risky financial advice, and extreme sports fine-tunes; does not test harmless reward hacks or number sequences.
Does not test whether RL induces broad misalignment; RL appears only in analyses of harmful-response separability.
Measures overlap and causal contribution of sparse parameters, not a shared linear direction or persona feature.
Tests pruning before fine-tuning, not requested-bad-behavior framing during training or brief benign retraining.
Does not report a size or training-stage robustness analysis of emergent misalignment, or seed/coherence-filter comparisons of its size.

relationships.condition: Unpruned Llama3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-14B and Qwen2.5-32B Instruct fine-tuned on bad medical advice, extreme sports or risky financial advice (Turner et al. data, 5,000 examples)
relationships.reason: From the text, not rows. Fig 6a/20 show nonzero coherent out-of-domain EM rates (roughly 0.05–0.26, figure only), with Table 20 examples. No non-fine-tuned or benign-FT control EM rate is given.
relationships.display_finding: The fine-tuned models showed nonzero coherent out-of-domain misalignment of roughly 0.05–0.26, with example responses; no rate is given for non-fine-tuned or benign fine-tuned controls.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Same-domain fine-tuning on bad medical advice, extreme sports, or risky financial advice across the three tested instruct models
reader_labels.reason: The study reports that these narrow fine-tunes produce out-of-domain EM and that EM-targeted pruning substantially reduces it in every condition (em-in-* rows).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Transfer of pruning effects between fine-tuning domains on Qwen2.5-14B-Inst and Qwen2.5-32B-Inst
reader_labels.reason: Cross-domain reductions vary substantially, including partial reductions such as -11%, -14%, and -30%; the authors describe transfer as occurring in most cases, not uniformly strongly (em-x-* rows).
